headline: Gaka is 画 (ga, “picture, drawing, painting”) plus 家 (-ka, “expert, professional, performer”), first cited to 1799.
Sei, “true”, is from Middle Chinese 正, the kan'on reading, so likely not as old as the shō reading.
Josei was repurposed from nyoshō in the Meiji period (1868–1912), using the newer kan'on readings.
Yubi is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *oyonpE.
Heiwa is a rearrangement of 和平 (wahei, “peace”), first attested in the Meiji era.
Mimau is 見 (mi) plus 舞う (mau).
Bussō is a pseudo-loan from Chinese, a reformation of 物騒がしい (monosawagashii).
Kuwaeru is from Classical Japanese 咥ふ (kufafu), possibly related to 食う (kuu, “to eat; to grab with one's mouth”).
Kazoku is from Middle Chinese 家族, but is not attested until 1808, so possibly a borrowing from modern written Chinese.
Seikō is from Middle Chinese 成功.
Kijun is 規 (ki, “compass”) plus 準 (jun, “spirit level”).
Kyū, “urgent”, is from Middle Chinese 急 (MC kip), and went through three sound changes.
Dai, “title”, is from Middle Chinese 題.
Kurashi is the continuative stem of 暮らす (kurasu, “to live, to lead a life”).
Noberu is from the classical lower bigrade verb のぶ (nobu), cognate with 伸べる (noberu) and 延べる (noberu).
Dakedo is だ (da, auxiliary expressing certainty) plus けど (kedo, “although”), first cited to 1907.
Yopparai is the continuative stem of 酔っ払う (yopparau).
Shimau is from the root shim-, cognate with 締む (shimu, “to fasten, tighten”) and 閉まる (shimaru, “to be closed”).
Usagi is from Proto-Japonic *osanki, possibly cognate with Goguryeo 烏斯含 (*osegam), and “highly likely a regional Wanderwort”.
Moshimoshi is a reduplication of もし (moshi), a shortened form of 申し (mōshi), from 申す (mōsu, “to speak”, humble).
En began as wen, from Middle Chinese 圓 (“circle”); the yen sense came in the Meiji period from 銀圓 (yínyuán), “round silver object(s)”.
Shihai is from Middle Chinese 支配 (MC tsye phwojH).
Oyoso is from おおよそ (ōyoso).
Kaisuiyoku is 海水 (kaisui, “seawater”) plus 浴 (yoku, “bathing”).
Mizugi is 水 (mizu, “water”) plus 着 (-gi, “wear, clothes”), first attested in 1908.
Saji was originally 茶 (sa, “tea”, the Tang reading) plus 匙 (ji, “spoon, scoop”), then re-interpreted as kun'yomi.
Sabaku, “desert”, was borrowed from Middle Chinese /*ʂamɑk̚/ as /*sabaku/.
Gaku is from Middle Chinese 額 (MC ngaek).
Mimai is the continuative stem of 見舞う (mimau), equivalent to 見 (mi) plus 舞い (mai).
Kiiroi is 黄色 (kiiro) plus い (-i).
Shokumotsu is Middle Chinese 食物, literally “eat + thing”, possibly altered from the goon reading jikimotsu.
